segments: Chronography of Barhebraeus. The reply being prepared and written,
the king personally handed over to them the document of the reply,
and dismissed them.
And he commanded, and twenty thousand zuzas were given to each of them.
And he sent with them ambassadors of his own,
and with them {OCR?} one hundred and seventy thousand gold dinars for the ransom of the Arab prisoners;
because the Arabs in the hands of the Romans were far more numerous than the Romans in the hands of the Arabs.
However, when the ambassadors went, the emperor of the Romans was unwilling to exchange prisoners or to ransom [them].
And in the year 308,
308 of the Arabs,
the foot-soldiers rioted,
(foot-soldiers,
infantrymen) (couriers?) of the Arabs in Baghdad;
and they broke down the gate of the prison,
and let out the evildoers.
And they laid hands on the Christians,
and plundered the residence of Abdallah bar Shim'on the physician,
and the residences of other Christian notables.
Then the governor gathered the executioners,
and seized the robbers,
and crucified their leader,
and cut off the hands of his associates.
And in the year 309,
309 of the Arabs, an ascetic {OCR?} man of the Arabs named al-Hallaj was arrested in Baghdad.
He called himself God incarnate,
and pretended to perform wonders through sleight of hand.
And the king commanded,
and they scourged him with a thousand lashes.
And afterwards they cut off his hands and his feet,
and burned his corpse;
as for his head, they hung it on a spear,
and also sent it around Persia.
And in the year 1238 [of the Greeks],
1238, the army of the Romans went out and reached as far as Samosata;
and they erected the emperor's tent in the Great Mosque that was in it,
and struck the clappers in it,
and took captives and left.
And the army of the Arabs pursued them,
and recovered some of the plunder,
and captured a man of the emperor of the Romans' kin,
and brought him as a prisoner to Baghdad.
Now Mu'nis the eunuch,
having gained renown in many wars, so that he was even surnamed 'al-Muzaffar'—that is to say, 'the Victorious'—
perceived jealousy on the part of the king.
And he feared treachery,
and began to be on his guard;
and hatred was revealed {OCR?}.
And the grandees and the majority of the soldiers adhered to him,
and encouraging him, they said:
"Why are you afraid? Behold, until a beard grows for you, we will wage war before you"—
that is to say, forever.
